planned-order.definition: A planned order is what we intend to buy from a supplier, or intend to make, and when. It isn't placed yet. The plan raises one so the projected balance stays at or above safety stock. Also called a planned supply order. Why it matters: planned orders show your future buying and production ahead of time, which is very useful for supplier forecasts, cash and capacity planning, and confirming lead times early. Review them before they become supply orders.

time-phased-planning.definition: Time-phased planning projects stock forward, bucket by bucket, against the forecast, open orders and lead times, and times a planned order so it arrives before the projected balance falls below safety stock.
time-phased-planning.example: The supply lead time is 6 weeks and the projected balance goes below safety stock in week 9. The plan shows the order in week 3, while the balance today can still look comfortable.
time-phased-planning.why: Today's balance only says whether you are short now. The projection shows a shortage that is already inside the lead time, and it shows an open order that arrives too late to cover it.

projected-stock.definition: Projected stock, also called the projected balance, is the on-hand quantity carried forward through each time bucket after that bucket's forecast and open supply orders.
projected-stock.example: Opening stock is 100. The week 1 forecast is 30 and nothing is due in, so the projected balance finishes week 1 at 70. Week 2 opens at 70. Its forecast is 40 and a supply order of 100 is due, so the projected balance finishes week 2 at 130.
projected-stock.why: The week the projected balance falls below safety stock is the week a planned order has to cover. Adding up all stock and all demand can hide that week, because supply that arrives later does not help an earlier bucket.

blocks.text: An expedite recommendation is triggered when projected inventory falls below safety stock before an existing open supply order arrives.
In simple terms:

items: Projected inventory drops below safety stock
An open supply order is due in a later period

blocks.text: A reschedule-out recommendation is triggered when an open supply order is due before it's needed.
In simple terms:

items: Projected inventory stays above safety stock without that order
An open supply order is due in an earlier period than needed
MRP recommends moving that order out to the period when projected inventory would otherwise drop below safety stock

That's logically correct, but it isn't worth acting on, and dozens of small messages can hide the ones that matter. Find the sweet spot: set your time buckets or a minimum change so that only meaningful moves show up.

Widgets come in cartons of 24, and you can't buy half a carton. If you need 30, you have to order 48, which is 2 cartons.
Lot sizes come in many forms: a full pallet (say 40 cartons), a set number of drums that fit on a truck (say 80 drums of 200 litres), or a full container load (FCL) from an overseas supplier.

The key question is how much demand one lot covers. If a carton is a few days' or a week's worth of demand, rounding up makes little difference. If one lot covers months of demand, every order leaves you with extra stock, which ties up cash and space and raises the risk it becomes slow-moving or obsolete.
To check, divide the lot size by average weekly demand. For example, cartons of 24 with demand of 12 a week means each carton is 2 weeks of cover.

If it's months of demand, for example 6 months, you end up holding far more stock than you need, which ties up cash, takes up space, and raises the risk the stock becomes slow-moving or obsolete.
To check, divide the MOQ by average weekly demand. For example, an MOQ of 1,000 with demand of 50 a week is 20 weeks of cover.

mrp.definition: MRP is a time-phased inventory planning process that projects future inventory balances over time.

blocks.text: MRP is a time-phased inventory planning process that projects future inventory balances over time.
At a simple level, MRP does this calculation for each item at each location, for each time period, such as each week:

items: Starting stock on hand (SOH) at that location
Plus incoming supply due to that location in that period
Minus expected demand from that location for that period
Resulting in projected ending inventory at that location for that period

blocks.text: The projected ending inventory from one period then becomes the starting inventory for the next period.
Large ERP systems usually calculate in daily buckets, while simpler planning tools often use weekly or monthly buckets.
Each location is planned on its own. Unless a source-destination relationship is set up in MRP, stock at one warehouse doesn't cover demand at another.

past-due.definition: Demand or supply that should already have happened by its date but hasn't.

blocks.text: Demand or supply that should already have happened by its date but hasn't.
A purchase order due on 1 July that hasn't arrived by 2 July is past-due.
Sales orders can be past-due too. They're usually called back orders.
**Why it matters:**
The key question is whether a past-due order will still happen, and when.

items: **Purchase orders:** any supplier, local or overseas, might have lost your order or never received it. Overseas orders also have more genuine reasons to run late, such as a delayed ship, a busy port, or goods held in customs. So a late overseas order is more likely to still be on its way, while a late local order is a stronger sign that something has gone wrong. Either way, check with the supplier and get a new date.

**Sales orders:** in some industries, a customer will wait weeks for a back order. In others, the sale is lost after a short delay. Check whether old back orders are still wanted before planning stock for them.

Stockturns show how much working capital is tied up in stock to meet customer demand at the service level you've chosen. More turns means less cash tied up in stock. Fewer turns means more cash tied up in stock.

blocks.text: **Customer service level:**

This is the share of demanded units you aim to supply straight from stock, without back orders or lost sales. For example, a 95% service level means that for every 100 units customers order, you aim to ship 95 from stock on hand.

The higher the service level you need, the more safety stock you have to hold. The cost also climbs steeply near the top: going from 95% to 99% takes much more extra stock than going from 90% to 95%. So it's worth setting higher targets for your most important items and lower ones for the rest.
Safety stock is generally designed to absorb normal operational variability, not extreme or exceptional events.

exception-outlier.definition: An exception is any event that causes recorded sales to differ from normal customer demand.

blocks.text: An exception is any event that causes recorded sales to differ from normal customer demand.

Exceptions may increase recorded sales, reduce recorded sales, or prevent genuine customer demand from being captured. If these events are not identified, they can distort the demand pattern used for forecasting.

Statistical forecasting assumes that past demand is a reasonable indicator of future demand. When unusual events are included in the sales history, they can distort this relationship and produce forecasts that are either too high or too low.
Identifying exceptions helps separate one-off events from the underlying demand pattern that the forecast is trying to predict.
Examples of exceptions include:
Not every unusual sale should be treated as an exception. The objective is to identify events that are unlikely to occur again under normal trading conditions.

forecast.definition: Forecasting is the process of estimating future demand for a product.

blocks.text: Forecasting is the process of estimating future demand for a product.
Forecasts help organizations plan inventory, purchasing, production, capacity, and supply requirements before actual customer orders occur.

A forecast is your best estimate of what customers will want to buy. It isn't a promise of what you can supply. Limits on working capital, manufacturing capacity, or other constraints can mean you're able to supply less than the forecast.
Most supply chains require time to respond to demand.
Because materials often have lead times, companies must make inventory and supply decisions before actual demand is known.
Forecasting helps organizations:
Organizations may use different forecast methods depending on the business.
Common examples include:

items: Statistical forecasts based on historical demand
Forecasts from account managers / product managers

blocks.text: Forecasts are estimates and will rarely be perfectly accurate.
Some level of normal variation between forecast and actual demand is expected in nearly all supply chains.
Demand variability, seasonality, promotions, market changes, and unexpected events can all affect forecast accuracy.
The objective is not perfect accuracy, but forecasts that are directionally useful and operationally reliable.
Consistent forecast bias is often more problematic than normal forecast variation.
Repeatedly over-forecasting may create excess inventory, while repeated under-forecasting may increase shortages and expedite activity.
In many planning environments, forecasts are gradually replaced by actual customer orders as demand becomes known.
Poor forecast quality can lead to:
While normal forecast error is expected, forecasts that are consistently inaccurate or heavily biased become far less useful for planning purposes.
In most supply chain environments, it is often more important that a forecast is operationally useful than perfectly accurate.
Forecasts are commonly more accurate at higher levels of aggregation than at detailed item or customer levels.

Forecast performance should therefore be monitored and continuously improved over time, with particular attention given to reducing systematic forecast bias.
Forecasting is fundamentally the process of separating signal from noise.
Historical sales contain both genuine demand patterns (the signal) and random variation (the noise).
By focusing on consistent patterns rather than isolated events, the resulting forecast is generally more representative of underlying customer demand.

The quality of the forecast is heavily influenced by the quality of the Sales History used as input. Reviewing exceptions and maintaining representative Sales History will generally improve forecast quality more than changing forecasting parameters.
